raw_case_text:
A 23-year-old man was admitted to the Emergency Department following a 5-day history of fever with myalgia in calf muscles, jaundice, a purpuric rash on his feet, haematemesis, and anuria for 2 days.
There was no medical, surgical, or contributory medical history. The patient did not drink alcohol, smoke, or use illicit drugs. There was no travel history, but the patient reported fishing in rivers regularly and had been bitten by a ferret in the 15 days preceding presentation. Laboratory findings in the emergency ward were: haemoglobin 80 g/L, white blood cell count (WBC) 22 x 109 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 13 x 109 cells/L, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 174 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 110 IU/L, total bilirubin 28 mg/dL, international normalised ratio (INR) 2.7, serum creatinine 6 mg/dL, serum urea 106 mg/dL.
Antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and spiramycin was initially started after computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax and abdomen showed diffuse micronodular interstitial syndrome. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit due to acute liver failure and anuria that required continuous venous haemafiltration, (CVVH) therapy.
Hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C viruses were excluded by hepatitis-virus-panel investigation. There was no laboratory evidence of infection with Epstein-Barr virus, or Cytomegalovirus. Serum paracetamol concentration was less than 1 mg/L. Ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, ferritin and an autoimmune screen were all unremarkable.
Based on the epidemiological context, compatible symptoms and biological results, an icterohaemorrhagic leptospirosis (Weil's disease) was suspected. This diagnosis was rapidly confirmed by positive leptospira serology combining IgM enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay method (ELISA), and microscopic agglutination test (MAT), as well as quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of blood and urine performed 7 days after the onset of symptoms. The patient was then treated with ceftriaxone alone for 2 weeks.
In the following days, the patient continued to have haematemesis and epistaxis. Liver involvement was mainly marked by cholestasis, with a maximum of total bilirubin at 65.9 mg/dL, AST at 524 IU/L, and ALT at 432 IU/L.
On the 10th day, the patient experienced haemorrhagic shock caused by bleeding from the pancreaticoduodenal artery. The patient had an asymptomatic median arcuate ligament syndrome, responsible for the development of numerous collateral fragile arteries. The haemorrhagic shock was controlled by embolisation of the pancreaticoduodenal artery.
Whilst the situation was stable, despite the persistence of liver and kidney failure, a gastroscopy was performed on the 30th day due to the appearance of melena. It found a complete ischemic necrosis of the duodenum with perforation, which was treated with a cephalic duodenopancreatectomy.
A deterioration was then noted, with major cytolysis and rapid development of acute liver failure (AST 16650 IU/L, ALT 7900 IU/L, total bilirubin 17 mg/dL, INR 3.12), requiring urgent orthotopic liver transplantation only 2 days later. Despite liver transplantation, the patient died 3 days after transplantation (36th day of hospitalisation) due to multiorgan failure and primary liver graft dysfunction.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 23-year-old male presenting with a 5-day history of fever, calf myalgia, jaundice, purpuric rash on the feet, hematemesis, and 2 days of anuria.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented to the emergency department after 5 days of fever, calf myalgias, jaundice, purpura on the feet, hematemesis, and 2 days of anuria. He was admitted and transferred to the ICU for acute liver failure and anuria requiring continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH). Despite targeted antimicrobial therapy, he had persistent bleeding (hematemesis, epistaxis, and severe cholestasis). On hospital day 10, he suffered hemorrhagic shock from pancreaticoduodenal artery bleeding treated via transcatheter arterial embolization. On day 30, melena prompted gastroscopy showing ischemic duodenal necrosis with perforation, requiring cephalic duodenopancreatectomy. He then developed hyperacute liver failure with massive cytolysis, necessitating emergency orthotopic liver transplantation on day 33, but died of primary graft dysfunction and multiorgan failure on day 36.
subjective.past_medical_history: No previous medical, surgical, or contributory history. Did not drink alcohol, smoke, or use illicit drugs. Epidemiological exposure: No travel history, but reported fishing in rivers regularly and had been bitten by a ferret 15 days prior to presentation.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination revealed severe jaundice, purpuric rash on both feet, severe calf muscle tenderness, hematemesis, epistaxis, and anuria. On day 10, he developed hemorrhagic shock.
objective.routine_investigations:
Emergency department labs: Hemoglobin 80 g/L, WBC 22 x 10^9 cells/L (neutrophils 90%), platelet count 13 x 10^9 cells/L, AST 174 IU/L, ALT 110 IU/L, total bilirubin 28 mg/dL, INR 2.7, serum creatinine 6 mg/dL, serum urea 106 mg/dL.
Subsequent peak labs: Total bilirubin reached 65.9 mg/dL, AST 524 IU/L, ALT 432 IU/L.
Pre-transplant deterioration (day 32): AST 16,650 IU/L, ALT 7,900 IU/L, total bilirubin 17 mg/dL, INR 3.12.
Negative routine/differential workup: Hepatitis A, B, and C viral panels negative; EBV and CMV serologies negative; serum paracetamol <1 mg/L; ceruloplasmin, alpha-1-antitrypsin, ferritin, and autoimmune screen all unremarkable.
objective.advanced_workup:
CT of thorax and abdomen: Diffuse micronodular interstitial pulmonary syndrome and median arcuate ligament syndrome with fragile arterial collaterals.
Transcatheter angiography: Active hemorrhage from pancreaticoduodenal artery, treated with embolization.
Upper endoscopy / gastroscopy (day 30): Complete ischemic necrosis of the duodenum with perforation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed severe icterohemorrhagic leptospirosis (Weil's disease) complicated by profound cholestatic jaundice, acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, diffuse alveolar pulmonary syndrome, pancreaticoduodenal hemorrhage, duodenal necrosis/perforation, and secondary hyperacute liver failure. Confirmed 7 days post-onset by positive Leptospira IgM ELISA, positive microscopic agglutination test (MAT), and positive quantitative PCR in blood and urine. Viral hepatitis (A, B, C, EBV, CMV), acetaminophen toxicity, and autoimmune liver disease were ruled out. Ferret bite and freshwater river exposure identified as transmission sources.
Plan & Outcome: Initial empiric therapy with IV ceftriaxone and spiramycin, followed by targeted IV ceftriaxone monotherapy for 2 weeks. Supported with CVVH, transcatheter arterial embolization, cephalic duodenopancreatectomy, and emergency orthotopic liver transplantation. Despite aggressive multidisciplinary interventions, the patient died on hospital day 36 from primary liver graft dysfunction and multiorgan failure.
